requests.description:
Exchanges credentials for a token pair.

**Unknown user and wrong password return an identical 401.** Distinguishing
them would turn this endpoint into a username oracle.

403 is returned only *after* the credentials are verified, when the account is
not `Active`. Requiring a valid password to learn that an account exists keeps
enumeration closed while still giving a disabled user a truthful message
instead of "wrong password". The `System` account can never satisfy either
check: its stored hash is not a valid PHC string, so no password verifies.

requests.description:
**The only endpoint that carries the type -> category link.**

`GET /unit-classes` returns each class with its `unit_type`, but that object is the shared
lookup shape, which deliberately carries no parent — so a client holding a class can reach
its **type** and stop there. `unit_types.id_unit_category` exists in the database and is
invisible through `/helpers`, which excludes domain columns so that one column list and one
scan can cover every lookup table.

That made the taxonomy unreachable in one direction: **Kategori could not be resolved from
Tipe or from Kelas by any endpoint.** This one closes the chain, so a breadcrumb
Domain > Kategori > Tipe > Kelas > Aset can be rendered from API data instead of a mapping
hardcoded in the client.

Read-only. Unit types are seeded master data an operator picks from; no route authors them.

requests.description:
The KATEGORI column of the taxonomy screen: every category, with how many types sit
DIRECTLY beneath it.

**THE COUNT IS OF THE LEVEL BELOW, NOT OF EVERYTHING BENEATH.** A category reports its
types, a type its classes (`GET /unit-types`), and a class its hulls
(`UnitClassSummary.hull_count`). That is what lets a drill-down add up: the numbers beside
the rows of one column sum to the header count of the next.

**Why this is not a flag on `/helpers`.** `unit_categories` IS served there — but through
the shared lookup shape, which is deliberately one structure across every lookup table. A
per-table `type_count` would make it eleven shapes and force every consumer to know which
one it was holding. A count describes the TAXONOMY rather than the lookup row, so it
belongs on a route that owns the taxonomy.

**No paging.** Ten-odd rows are drawn in full, and a page of a picker is an incomplete
picker.

## Filtering by service branch

`?id_service_branch=<id>` returns only the categories that branch OWNS. Omit it for every
category.

**Ownership is declared, not derived.** Which categories a branch counts is a mapping the
CMS authors, not a query over the hulls that happen to exist — so a branch shows its
categories even while it holds no hulls of that kind. The taxonomy is a plan, and a plan an
empty warehouse cannot express is not much of one.

**A branch that owns nothing, and an id that names no branch, both return `[]`** — the same
deliberately-unhelpful answer as `?id_unit_category` on `/unit-types`, for the same reason:
the screen draws a row per category and an empty list renders correctly, whereas an error
would have to be reconciled.

**`?id_service_branch=0` is NOT rejected: it returns every category.** The field is a plain
integer, so zero is indistinguishable from the parameter being absent, and the
`minimum: 1` below is therefore declarative rather than enforced for zero. A client sending
zero sees the whole taxonomy, which reads in the UI as "this branch owns everything". Send
the parameter or leave it out; do not send zero.

A NON-NUMERIC value is refused with **422**, not 400.

## Authoring

Since migration 000024 the taxonomy is operator-authorable: `POST` here, plus `PATCH` and
`DELETE` on `/unit-categories/{id}`. This paragraph used to read "Read-only. Categories are
seeded master data; no route authors them", which was true when it was written.

**A SEEDED ROW IS NOT PROTECTED BY THE SERVER.** Every category 000002 seeded carries
`is_system: true`, and that flag is a SIGNAL TO THE CLIENT rather than a rule the API
enforces — the same arrangement `DELETE /hierarchy/{id}` has. A caller holding the delete
action CAN remove a seeded category. **Disable the delete affordance on `is_system` rows;**
nothing here will stop it.

One thing does limit the damage, and it is not a substitute for that: a category with unit
types under it is refused with `409` by the foreign key. Every seeded category has at least
one type today, so they are all covered by it — this is the table where the foreign key
happens to be sufficient.

**There is no soft delete.** A delete is a delete and the row is gone. Migration 000019
records the reason for the equivalent table: `is_system` already marks what a migration wrote,
and a tombstone beside it would be a second, quieter way to hide a row.

The CMS's top-level inventory tabs: one count per service branch.

**THE COUNT IS OF LIVE HULLS**, which is what the drill-down eventually selects. The taxonomy

requests.description:
Requires the `read` action on `/system/unit-classes`. The pictures ARE unit-class
data, so they share its permission rather than having one of their own — a separate
object would let the two drift into "you may edit a class but not its picture",
which reads as a CMS bug rather than as a policy decision.

**This is the one response in the document that is NOT the standard envelope.**
It is a binary zip: a client either saves it or unzips it, and neither can do
anything with a `data` wrapper around a zip.

The archive holds `manifest.json` FIRST — so it can be read from a stream without
buffering the whole archive or seeking to its end — followed by one entry per class
that has a picture.

## Caching

The `ETag` changes when, and only when, the CONTENT changes. Send it back as
`If-None-Match` and the usual answer is `304 Not Modified`, costing no image bytes
at all. Prefer `GET /assets/unit-class-images/manifest` for the check itself: it
carries the same ETag and weighs a few kilobytes.

Compare the tag, not the clock. HTTP `Date` has one-second resolution, so a
refresh landing in the same second as the previous one would appear unchanged.

requests.description:
Requires the `update` action on `/system/unit-classes`. A picture is a FIELD of a
class, so setting one and clearing one are the same capability — see DELETE below.

Send `multipart/form-data` with the picture in a part named **`file`**.

## What is accepted

PNG and JPEG, up to **5 MiB**. The limit is a blast-radius control rather than a
storage one: every client downloads the whole archive, so one oversized picture is
a cost paid by every desktop in the fleet.

The declared `Content-Type` is **not trusted**. The format recorded is the one the
server's decoder identified, because a decoder's answer is a fact and the request's
is a claim. Bytes that are not a readable image are refused whatever the header
said.

Pixel dimensions are checked BEFORE the image is expanded, and it is refused if
either side exceeds 10000 px or the total exceeds 40 megapixels. A few hundred
kilobytes of PNG can declare sixty thousand pixels a side, and decoding that would
exhaust the server's memory — so the bounds are applied to the header, not after a
decode that has already happened.

## Replacing

An upload replaces the previous picture. The new object is written BEFORE the old
one is removed, so a failure at any point leaves the class on a working picture
rather than on none.

requests.description:
Requires `create` on `/system/hierarchy`.

**THE INTERESTING CASE IS INSERTING IN THE MIDDLE.** A future Koarmada belongs between Gugus
and Operasi Gabungan, and a level below Unsur is the same problem at the other end, so the
request says WHERE the new level goes rather than what number it gets. The server renumbers.

`insert_after_id` names the level the new one ranks **directly above**, so one field covers
all three positions:

| `insert_after_id` | result |
|---|---|
| omitted | the new level becomes the LOWEST, below everything |
| any id | the new level sits immediately above that level |
| the highest level's id | the new level becomes the HIGHEST, above everything |

"After" reads against this list as a client displays it — lowest first — so the new level
appears immediately after the named one. Sending a raw `echelon_rank` instead would put the
dense numbering and the renumbering it needs in the caller's hands.

**400 if `insert_after_id` names a level that does not exist.** There is deliberately no
fallback to the top or the bottom: a client holding a stale list would otherwise renumber
every level in the system while the operator watched for a reason they could not see.

**409 if the name is already in use.** Names are unique across the vocabulary.

**THE NEW LEVEL IS NEVER A SYSTEM ROW**, so the CMS may offer to remove it. The four seeded
levels carry `is_system`, which stops the default hierarchy being deleted and leaving a
system whose vocabulary is a blank page.

requests.description:
Accepts up to 60 fixes from one vessel's beacon. This is the endpoint the mobile app calls.

**Authorised by being this vessel's current commander — not by a permission.** A Casbin
object names a resource family and carries no instance id, so "may this user report for
THIS ship" is not expressible as a policy. The check is an instance comparison in the
service, and the same reasoning applies to `GET /live-feed/me`.

A refusal is **403, not 404**: the vessel exists and the caller may have listed it a moment
earlier, so reporting a blocked report as "not found" would hide it from the audit trail.
Only a vessel that genuinely does not exist is a 404.

## What the server does with `recorded_at`

The client sends when it *believes* it observed each fix; the server decides whether that
is a live report or a backlog.

| Gap from the server's clock | Treatment |
|---|---|
| within ±60 s | **live** — `recorded_at` is re-stamped with the server's time |
| older than 60 s, within 30 days | **backfill** — the device's `recorded_at` is kept |
| older than 30 days | **refused**, counted in `rejected` |

Re-stamping a live fix is not tidiness. A `recorded_at` in the future would become the
vessel's latest position, and the guard that discards out-of-order fixes would then discard
every honest fix until real time caught up — a ship reporting steadily that never moves on
the map. A device clock more than a minute ahead is therefore treated as live, re-stamped,
and logged as a warning.

Keeping a backfill's own timestamp is the mirror of the same argument: a backlog's whole
value is *where the vessel was when it could not report*, and re-stamping it to now would
draw a straight line the ship never sailed.

## Rejections

Age is the only per-fix refusal, and it is permanent — an out-of-retention fix cannot be
made valid by sending it again. The response therefore carries **counts**, not a list of
complaints with nothing to act on. A batch in which every fix was refused is still a
**200**: the request was understood and each fix was examined, and the counts are the
answer.

## Ordering

Fixes may arrive in any order, and the vessel's latest position is taken from the **newest
fix in the batch by `recorded_at`** — not the last one sent. A backlog flushed after a
reconnect interleaves old points among new ones, so the last one sent is frequently not the
newest one observed.

requests.description:
**Reached by authentication alone — no application permission.** Two kinds of caller arrive
here, and the service decides between them IN THIS ORDER:

1. a **participant** — anyone holding a place in this game. They see it through the rules
   below, which means `area` and `map_tag` are withheld until the exercise starts.
2. **staff** — a caller holding `read` on `/system/games`, who sees all of it. An operator
   reviewing a plan is not a participant, and withholding the area from them during
   Preparation would withhold it precisely when the Game Master is placing units against it.

A caller who is neither is refused with **403** — not 404, because the game plainly exists
and they may have seen it in a list a moment ago.

The participant check runs FIRST, and the order is a security decision rather than a
preference: an administrator who is also playing a Commando is treated as the participant
they are, so the area stays withheld during Preparation and the game is refused at Closure.

The response depends on WHO is asking and WHICH state the game is in. Two fields are
withheld from participants rather than being absent from the schema:

* `area` and `map_tag` are returned to the Game Master and Judges at every state, and to
  Commandos and unit personnel only from `execution` onward. The concept is explicit:
  personnel "does not know where the 'Game Area' is until it is Executed".

They are OMITTED, not nulled, which is why both are optional in the schema. A participant
during Preparation still needs the name and state to render "waiting for readiness", so
refusing the whole resource would deny them information they are entitled to.

In `closure` this endpoint is refused to participants entirely — 403. That is a different
mechanism from withholding: the concept ejects personnel from Closure, so there is
nothing in that state they may see.

There is no mode-conditional exception here any more. The note that used to sit at this
point concerned Operational, where withholding the area bought nothing because a Commando
was physically inside it — and Operational is no longer a game mode at all. The rule now
applies to every game there is, so it needs no exception.

requests.description:
Authorised by being **this game's Game Master**, not by an application permission.

The route itself carries no permission middleware, so any authenticated caller can REACH it
and only the game's own Game Master is obeyed. That is a widening of who may ask and a
narrowing of who is answered: before participants existed, an administrator was the only
caller who could get here, and any administrator could run any game.

That distinction is the whole reason this is not a `PATCH` on the game. Creating a game is
an application capability — an operator holds `create` on `/system/games` — while running
one is in-game authority, which comes from a participant assignment and is scoped to a
single game. A Casbin object cannot express "the Game Master of THIS game", so the check
is an instance comparison in the service, and a failure is **403, not 404**.

Forward-only, one step at a time:

| From | To | Precondition |
|------|----|--------------|
| `planning` | `preparation` | none — the Game Master decides planning is done |
| `preparation` | `execution` | at least one unit assigned, at least one participant on the exercise side, and every one of them ready |
| `execution` | `closure` | none — the Game Master ends the exercise |

Judges are excluded from the readiness precondition, which is also what makes B5's
"more lenient readiness gate" for Static a statement about a baseline rather than a new
mechanism.

**The gate has three parts, and the last two are the ones that are easy to leave out.** An
exercise that is READY but has no hulls assigned has nothing to manoeuvre, nothing to give an
order to, and no unit for a Commando to lead. And a roster of nothing but Judges satisfies
"everyone is ready" vacuously. The refusal names every missing ingredient at once, under
`data.errors`, rather than the first one found — a freshly created game is missing two of
them, and reporting one per attempt would make the Game Master press Advance twice to learn
two things.

Note also that a **role change clears readiness**, so a game can be refused by a declaration
the caller did not withdraw.

A skipped step, a step backwards, or a step out of a game already in `closure`, is
**409**. Reporting it as a 400 would suggest the request was malformed; it was well-formed
and refused.

requests.description:
The room key is the ONLY input: the client does not know the game id yet, which is exactly
what this call is for. It answers with the game AND the caller's own participant row, so a
freshly installed app learns in one request what it has entered, what it may do there, and
whether it has already declared readiness.

**Authentication only.** What authorises the call is holding a place in the game the key
belongs to — an instance fact, which a Casbin object cannot express because objects name
resource families and carry no instance id.

**A wrong key is 404** — the same 404 a discarded game produces, so the endpoint cannot be
used to tell a key that never existed from one whose exercise was cancelled.

**A valid key held by a non-participant is 403.** Not 404: they hold a real key, so the room
plainly exists, and telling them otherwise would send them hunting for a typo in a key that
is correct. The remedy is to ask the Game Master for a place, and only a 403 says that. It
leaks nothing — a guessed key is never the valid one, so somebody guessing only ever sees
the 404.

**Refused at `closure`** for a participant the rules eject from it, on the same terms as
`GET /games/{id}`. Both refusals exist because one is not enough: a participant who cannot
READ a game must not be able to enter it through the other door either.

The key is stored unhashed, unlike every other secret in this API, because it is
TRANSCRIBED — read aloud or copied off a board and typed into a handset — and a hash cannot
be read out. Migration 000017 records that as a decision rather than an oversight.

description:
Backend for the Indonesian Navy (TNI AL) Tactical Floor Game.

## Response envelope

Every response, success or failure, is the same envelope. A client therefore has
exactly one shape to unwrap and one place to read an error from.

```json
{ "status_code": 200, "message": "Successfull", "data": { }, "metadata": { } }
```

* `data` is `null` on a 5xx, and on a 4xx when the failure is not attributable to a
  named input.
* `metadata` is present only on paginated list endpoints.

**One response in this document is NOT the envelope:**
`GET /assets/unit-class-images` returns a binary zip. A client either saves it or
unzips it, and neither can do anything with a `data` wrapper around a zip. Its 304
is likewise bodyless, as a 304 must be.

## Errors

Every 4xx and 5xx body is `ErrorResponse`. Field-level failures carry a map from
the **request field name** to a human-readable reason, keyed exactly as the client
sent it — so `{"errors": {"name": "This field is required."}}` refers to the `name`
field of the request body, not to any internal name.

| Status | Meaning                                                              |
|--------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 400    | The request parsed but a field failed validation — see `data.errors`. |
| 401    | No token, or a token that is expired or invalid.                      |
| 403    | Authenticated, but not permitted. Also: the account is not Active.     |
| 404    | The resource does not exist, or is soft-deleted.                       |
| 409    | A uniqueness constraint was violated (username, email, hull number).   |
| 422    | The body could not be parsed at all.                                  |
| 429    | Rate limited. `Retry-After` says how long to wait.                     |
| 500    | A defect on our side. The body never contains internal detail.         |

## Authentication

`Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` on everything except `/auth/login` and
`/auth/refresh`.

Refresh tokens are returned **both** as an `HttpOnly` cookie and, when the request
asks for it, in the response body. Browser clients should rely on the cookie;
mobile and desktop clients have no cookie jar and must use the body. See
`TokenPair.refresh_token`.
